research_question: For a BPR-trained factorization machine on implicit sparse categorical CTR/ranking data (evaluated on GAUC and nDCG@5), is uniform random within-user negative sampling known to underperform smarter negative sampling strategies — e.g. hard-negative mining (selecting negatives the current model already scores highly), dynamic/adaptive negative sampling (WARP-style, sampling several candidates and keeping the highest-scoring one as the "hard" negative), or popularity-weighted negative sampling — and if so, is there a version of this that's cheap enough to compute per-minibatch on CPU (i.e., without a full re-scoring pass over the item catalog) that's known to reliably improve ranking metrics over vanilla BPR?
reflection: Adding the `tag` field barely moved primary (+0.0001, within noise) and, like the earlier weight-decay sweep, it overfits after epoch 6 — two turns in a row confirm we've plateaued on both "add one more categorical field" and "tune existing regularization/loss knob" as levers. Per the plateau warning, I should look outward rather than guess a third small variant of the same feature-adding or regularization mechanism.

note.title: Dynamic Negative Sampling (DNS) improves BPR over uniform sampling at minimal extra cost
note.citation: Zhang, Chen, Wang & Yu 2013, SIGIR ("Optimizing Top-N Collaborative Filtering via Dynamic Negative Item Sampling")
note.tags: BPR, dynamic negative sampling, DNS, hard negative mining, WARP, GAUC, nDCG, implicit feedback, factorization machine, sparse CTR ranking, popularity skew
note.body: Yes — uniform random negative sampling is well established to underperform hard/dynamic negative sampling for BPR-style pairwise ranking losses, and Dynamic Negative Sampling (DNS) is the standard cheap fix: for each positive, draw a small pool of N (e.g. 5–32) candidate negatives uniformly (optionally popularity-weighted) from the current minibatch or a light random draw, score just those N with the current model's forward pass, and keep the highest-scoring one as the "hard" negative for the BPR update — this needs only N extra dot-products per positive, not a catalog-wide rescoring pass, so it is CPU/minibatch-friendly. Weinan Zhang et al.'s original SIGIR 2013 paper (DNS) showed this consistently beats uniform BPR on top-N ranking metrics; later theoretical work (Lai et al., WWW 2023, "On the Theories Behind Hard Negative Sampling for Recommendation," arXiv:2302.03472) proves BPR+DNS is an exact estimator of One-way Partial AUC, explaining why it specifically sharpens top-heavy metrics like nDCG@k and GAUC rather than plain AUC. WARP (Weston et al.) is the closely related predecessor that samples until it finds a rank-violating negative rather than picking the max of a fixed pool; DNS(M=1,N) is described in the literature as a simplified, more predictable-cost variant of the same idea. For a KuaiRand-Pure-style sparse, popularity-skewed short-video task, combining DNS's in-pool hard-negative selection with popularity-aware candidate sampling (to avoid always picking globally-popular items as "hard" negatives, which can be false negatives / degenerate) is the commonly recommended cheap recipe; note the same line of work (and follow-ups like Enhanced BPR, arXiv:2403.19276) warns that pushing the pool size N too high increases false-negative risk on very sparse data, so N is typically kept small (≈5–20) precisely to stay cheap and stable on CPU.
